conclusions: Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}, Corollary~\ref{cor: ps-genfun}, and Proposition~\ref{prop: ps-computation} hold

nodes.name: Generating function for M-matrices
nodes.statement: \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\frac{S(z)}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1-z^{\phi_i\ell_i})}
nodes.label: eqn: ps-genfun

nodes.name: Polyhedral theorem for M-matrices
nodes.statement:
Theorem~\ref{thm: poly} then
holds as stated, defining~$\deg(\omega):=\phi\cdot\omega$ in part~\ref{poly3}.
conclusions: Theorem~\ref{thm: poly} then holds as stated

nodes.name: Facet proposition for M-matrices
nodes.statement:
Proposition~\ref{prop: facet} holds by again replacing~$\ell_i$
by~$\phi_i\ell_i$ and redefining~$\mathrm{ord}_q(v_i)$ as discussed above.

nodes.name: Multigrading by phi
nodes.statement:
To generalize the results in
Section~\ref{sect: molien}, take~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]$ to have the multigrading determined
by~$\deg(x_i):=\phi_i$ for~$i=1,\dots,n$.

nodes.name: Representation rho for M-matrices
nodes.statement: \rho(\chi)=(1,\chi([v_2-\deg(v_2)q]),\chi([v_3-\deg(v_3)q]),\dots,\chi([v_n-\deg(v_n)q])).
nodes.label: eqn: new rho

nodes.name: Invariant theorem for M-matrices
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm: invariants} then extends with no changes to its statement.
conclusions: Theorem~\ref{thm: invariants} then extends with no changes to its statement.

nodes.name: Multigraded Molien series for M-matrices
nodes.statement:
For
Corollary~\ref{cor: lambda-molien}, use a multigraded version of Molien's theorem,
for abelian groups, to get
\begin{equation} \Lambda_{[D]}(z)=
\Phi_{\Gamma,\chi}(z^{\phi_1},\dots,z^{\phi_n})
:=\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A})|}\sum_{\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A})^*}\frac{\overline{\chi([D])}}{\det(I_n-\mathrm{diag}(z^{\phi_1},\dots,z^{\phi_n})\rho(\chi))}
\end{equation}
where~$\mathrm{diag}(\,\cdot\,)$ denotes the diagonal matrix with the given diagonal entries.
assumptions: use a multigraded version of Molien's theorem, for abelian groups
nodes.statement_short: $\Lambda_{[D]}$ is a multigraded Molien series with $z^{\phi_i}$ in place of $z$.

nodes.name: Multigraded Molien formula
nodes.label: eqn: new lambda_molien

nodes.name: Cartan matrices are M-matrices
nodes.statement:
Let~$\Phi$ be a finite,
crystallographic, irreducible root system. The Cartan matrix~$C$ for~$\Phi$ is
an~$M$-matrix.
assumptions: Let~$\Phi$ be a finite, crystallographic, irreducible root system.
conclusions: The Cartan matrix~$C$ for~$\Phi$ is an~$M$-matrix.

nodes.name: Burning configurations of a Cartan matrix
nodes.statement:
Its burning configurations are the elements of the root lattice
lying in the fundamental chamber (with respect to a choice of simple roots).
conclusions: Its burning configurations are the elements of the root lattice lying in the fundamental chamber

nodes.name: Extended Cartan matrix
nodes.statement:
Making particular natural choices for burning configurations for~$C$ and its
transpose~$C^t$, the authors define the extended Cartan matrix~$\widetilde{C}$,
which is the Cartan matrix for the corresponding affine root system.

nodes.name: Picard group of extended Cartan matrix is the fundamental group
nodes.statement:
Letting~$A=C^t$ and~$\widehat{A}=\widetilde{C}^t$, it turns out that~$\mathrm{Pic}(\widehat{A})$ is the
fundamental group of~$\Phi$, i.e., the quotient of the weight lattice by the
root lattice.

nodes.name: Root system B_3
nodes.statement_short: For $B_3$: $\mathrm{Jac}\simeq\mathbb{Z}/2$, primary/secondary divisors and both forms of $\Lambda$.

nodes.name: McKay multiplicities m_ij
nodes.statement:
Let~$\rho\colon\Gamma\to\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}^n)$ be a faithful representation of a finite
group~$\Gamma$ with character~$\chi_{\rho}$.
Let~$\rho_1,\dots,\rho_n$ be the irreducible complex representations
of~$\Gamma$, with~$\rho_1$ the trivial representation, and with respective
characters~$\chi_1,\dots,\chi_n$.  For each~$i$,
denote the character of the tensor product
~$\rho\otimes\rho_i$ by~$\chi_{\rho}\cdot\chi_i$, and define integers~$m_{ij}$ by
\[
  \chi_{\rho}\cdot\chi_i=\sum_{j=1}^nm_{ij}\chi_i.
\]

nodes.name: Extended McKay-Cartan matrix
nodes.statement:
Define the~$n\times n$ matrix~$M:=(m_{ij})$ and the
{\em extended McKay-Cartan} matrix~$\widetilde{C}:=nI_n-M$.

nodes.name: McKay-Cartan matrix
Burning scripts for McKay-Cartan matrices
nodes.statement:
The vectors
$u=w=(\dim\rho_2,\dots,\dim\rho_n)$ are burning scripts for~$A$ and~$A^t$, with
respect to which~$\widehat{A}=\widetilde{C}^t$ with left and right kernel generators
\[
  \phi = \delta = (\dim\rho_1,\dots,\dim\rho_n).
\]

nodes.name: McKay quiver
nodes.statement:
The {\em McKay quiver} of~$\gamma$ is the directed graph with
vertices~$\chi_1,\dots,\chi_n$ and~$m_{ij}$ directed edges from~$\chi_i$
to~$\chi_j$ for each~$i,j$.

nodes.name: McKay quiver of the cycle-graph representation
nodes.statement:
Consider the representation~$\rho\colon\mathrm{Jac}(G)^*\to\mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}^n)$
  defined by~(\ref{rho}) of Section~\ref{sect: molien}.  When~$G=C_n$, the
  cyclic graph on~$n$-vertices,~$\rho$ is the regular representation of the
  cyclic group $\mathrm{Jac}(G)^*\simeq\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.  Therefore,~$m_{ij}=1$ for all~$i,j$,
  the McKay quiver may be thought of as the (undirected) complete graph~$K_n$
  on~$n$ vertices, and $\widehat{A}$ is its Laplacian matrix.
  Thus,~$\mathrm{Jac}(\widehat{A})=\mathrm{Jac}(K_n)$.

  More generally (\cite{BKR}, Section~6.2), the McKay quiver for any faithful complex
  representation~$\gamma$ of an abelian group has (directed) Laplacian matrix equal to the
  matrix~$\widehat{A}$ for~$\gamma$.

nodes.name: Combinatorial bijections for arbitrary n and k
nodes.statement:
It would be
interesting to find combinatorial bijections for arbitrary~$n$ and~$k$.

nodes.name: Enumeration for root systems and representations
nodes.statement:
It may be worthwhile to investigate the implications for each type of root
system or for certain classes of representations.

nodes.name: Tropical complete linear systems are cell complexes
nodes.statement:
If~$D$ is a
(tropical) divisor on~$\Gamma$ of degree~$k$, then the complete linear
system~$|D|$ can be realized as a cell complex in~$\mathrm{Sym}^k(\Gamma)$
(\cite{Gathmann}, \cite{Haase}, \cite{Mikhalkin}).
nodes.origin_citation: Gathmann & Kerber; Haase, Musiker & Yu; Mikhalkin & Zharkov
assumptions: If~$D$ is a (tropical) divisor on~$\Gamma$ of degree~$k$
conclusions: the complete linear system~$|D|$ can be realized as a cell complex in~$\mathrm{Sym}^k(\Gamma)$

nodes.name: Combinatorics of graph linear systems inside tropical cell complexes
nodes.statement:
While we have determined this
cardinality, one could hope to further describe the combinatorics of the
complete linear system for a divisor on~$G$ within the cell complex for the
associated divisor on~$\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Choose multiples
nodes.statement:
To prove part~\ref{ps-1}, for each~$v\in V$, let~$\ell_v$ be a
  positive multiple of~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$, and define~$\mathcal{P}$ and
  each~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ as in part~\ref{ps-2} of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Fix multiples $\ell_v$ of $\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$ and the candidate $\mathcal{P}$, $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$.

nodes.name: Construct decomposition
nodes.statement:
Given~$E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$, for each~$v\in V$, let~$k_v$ be the largest integer such
  that~$E(v)-k_v\ell_v\geq0$, and define~$F:=E-\sum_{v\in
  V}k_v\ell_vv\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$.  Then $E=F+\sum_{v\in V}k_v\ell_vv$ is a
  decomposition as required in part~\ref{ps-1}.
nodes.statement_short: Divide coordinates by $\ell_v$ to write $E=F+\sum k_v\ell_v v$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of decomposition
nodes.statement:
For uniqueness of this
  decomposition, suppose $E = F' + \sum_{v\in V}k_v'v$ for
  some~$F'\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ and~$k'_v\in\mathbb{N}$.  Then for each~$v\in V$, we
  have~$0\leq F(v)=E(v)- k_v\ell_v<\ell_v$ and~$0\leq F'(v)=E(v)-k'_v\ell_v<\ell_v$.
  Subtracting these inequalities yields $-\ell_v<(k'_v-k_v)\ell_v<\ell_v$.  It
  follows that~$k_v=k'_v$ for all~$v$ and~$F=F'$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare remainders to get $k_v=k'_v$ and $F=F'$.

nodes.name: Set up necessity
nodes.statement:
We have shown that if~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ have the form
  displayed in~$\ref{ps-2}$, then they serve as sets of primary and secondary
  divisors, i.e., they satisfy the conditions in part~\ref{ps-1}.  To show that
  necessity of this form and thus finish the proof of part~\ref{ps-2},
  let~$\mathcal{P}$ and~$\{\mathcal{S}_{[D]}\}_{[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)}$ be any sets of
  primary and~$[D]$-secondary divisors.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce part (2) to showing any primary/secondary system has the stated form.

nodes.name: Minimal m_v
nodes.statement:
Since~$\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ is finite, for
  each~$v\in V$, there is a smallest natural number~$m_v$ such
  that~$m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v\notin\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$.  Consider the primary-secondary
  decomposition~$m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v=F+\sum_{P\in\mathcal{P}}a_PP$. Since the divisors on
  the right-hand side are effective and all~$a_P$ are nonnegative, considering
  coefficients on both sides, it follows that decomposition takes the
  form~$m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v=av+bv$ for some~$a,b\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $av\in\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$
  and $bv\in\mathcal{P}$. By definition of~$m_v$, we must have~$b>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Take least $m_v$ with $m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)v\notin\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ and decompose it.

nodes.name: Rule out a' nonzero
nodes.statement:
Since~$\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ and~$\mathcal{P}$ are subsets of~$\mathbb{E}_{[0]}$, we
  have~$av\sim aq$ and~$bv\sim bq$.  Therefore,~$a=a'\mathrm{ord}(v)$ and~$b=b'\mathrm{ord}(v)$
  for some~$a',b'\in\mathbb{N}$.  If~$a'\neq0$, then~$b'<m_v$, which
  implies~$b'\mathrm{ord}(v)v\in\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ by definition of~$m_v$.  However, that
  is impossible since the uniqueness of decompositions described in
  part~\ref{ps-1} implies~$\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ and~$\mathcal{P}$ are disjoint.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients are multiples of $\mathrm{ord}(v)$; $a'\neq0$ contradicts disjointness of $\mathcal{S}_{[0]}$ and $\mathcal{P}$.

nodes.name: Conclude form of P and S
nodes.statement:
Defining~$\ell_v:=m_v\mathrm{ord}(v)$, it follows that~$\ell_v v\in\mathcal{P}$ for
  all~$v$.  However, again by uniqueness of decompositions, the elements
  of~$\mathcal{P}$ must be linearly independent over~$\mathbb{Z}$, which implies there are
  no other primary divisors.  So~$\mathcal{P}=\left\{ \ell_v:v\in V \right\}$, as
  claimed, and it is then straightforward to show that~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ must
  have the form stated in~\ref{ps-2} for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Linear independence forces $\mathcal{P}=\{\ell_v v\}$ and hence the form of $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$.

nodes.name: Multivariate generating function
nodes.statement:
Introduce indeterminates~$\left\{ x_v \right\}_{v\in V}$, and
  identify each effective divisor~$E$ with a monomial~$x^E:=\prod_{v\in
  V}x_v^{E(v)}$. Define
  \[
    \sigma_D(x)=\sum_{E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}}x^{E}.
  \]
nodes.statement_short: Encode $\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ as the monomial sum $\sigma_D(x)$.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement:
By Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}, we may uniquely write
  \[
    x^E=x^F\cdot\prod_{P\in\mathcal{P}}x^{a_PP} =x^F\cdot\prod_{v\in V}x_v^{a_v\ell_v}
  \]
  for some~$F\in\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ and~$a_v\geq0$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor each monomial uniquely as secondary times primary powers.

nodes.name: Sum geometric series
nodes.statement_short: Sum the geometric series in each $x_v^{\ell_v}$.

nodes.name: Specialize variables
nodes.statement: Now note that $\Lambda_{[D]}(z)=\sigma_D(z,z,\dots,z)$ to conclude the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Set all $x_v=z$.

nodes.name: Invertibility of reduced Laplacian
nodes.statement:
First note that~$\tilde{L}$ has rank~$n-1$, and thus has an
  inverse~$\tilde{L}^{-1}$ over~$\mathbb{Q}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\tilde L$ is invertible over $\mathbb{Q}$.

nodes.name: Order via inverse
nodes.statement:
By~\eqref{eqn: Jac(G)} of Section~\ref{sect: prelims}, the order of~$[v-q]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ is the least positive integer~$k$
  such that~$kv\in\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}$.  Therefore,~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ is the least positive
  integer~$k$ such that~$\tilde{L}^{-1}(kv)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$. Part~\ref{ps-comp1} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Order of $[v-q]$ is least $k$ with $\tilde L^{-1}(kv)$ integral, giving part (1).

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement:
Part~\ref{ps-comp2} is immediate: a divisor~$E$ is a standard representative
  for an element in~$H_{[D]}$ if and only if $E|_{q=0}=D|_{q=0} \bmod\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}$ and
  $0\leq E(v)<\ell_v$ for all~$v\in V$, which is exactly the requirement for
  being an element of~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$.
nodes.statement_short: Standard representatives of $H_{[D]}$ are exactly the secondary divisors.

nodes.name: Surjection onto Jac
nodes.statement:
Now consider part~\ref{ps-comp3}.
  Since~$\ell_v[v-q]=[0]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ for all~$v$, there is a surjection
  \[
    \textstyle \mathbb{Z}^n/\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v\mathbb{Z}\to\mathrm{Jac}(G)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}
  \]
  which sends the class of the~$v$-th standard basis vector to~$[v-q]$.
nodes.statement_short: Build the surjection $\mathbb{Z}^n/\prod\ell_v\mathbb{Z}\to\mathrm{Jac}(G)$.

nodes.name: Count for [0]
nodes.statement:
Its kernel is~$H_{[0]}$.  So by part~\ref{ps-comp2}, we have
  $|\mathcal{S}_{[0]}||\mathrm{Jac}(G)|=\prod_{v\in V}\ell_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel is $H_{[0]}$, so $|\mathcal{S}_{[0]}||\mathrm{Jac}|=\prod\ell_v$.

nodes.name: Translate to [D]
nodes.statement:
However, for
  each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$, there is a
  well-defined bijection
  \begin{align*}
    H_{[0]}&\to H_{[D]}\\
    \pi(E)&\mapsto\pi(D+E).
  \end{align*}
  So~$|\mathcal{S}_{[D]}|=|\mathcal{S}_{[0]}|$, and part~\ref{ps-comp3} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Translation $H_{[0]}\to H_{[D]}$ gives the same count for every class.

nodes.name: Compute orders
nodes.statement:
To summarize the above: in order to compute a set of primary
  divisors, use Proposition~\ref{prop: ps-computation} to compute
  each~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ for~$v\neq q$ from the columns of~$\tilde{L}^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute each $\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$ from the columns of $\tilde L^{-1}$ (Proposition 3.4).

nodes.name: Choose primary divisors
nodes.statement:
Then
  take~$\mathcal{P}=\{ \ell_v v \}_{v\in V}$ where the~$\ell_v$ are arbitrary
  positive multiples of the corresponding~$\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$.  In order to minimize
  the number of secondary divisors, one would take~$\ell_v=\mathrm{ord}_{q}(v)$ for
  each~$v$.  In particular, this would mean~$\ell_q=\mathrm{ord}_{q}(q)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $\mathcal{P}=\{\ell_v v\}$, ideally with $\ell_v=\mathrm{ord}_q(v)$.

nodes.name: Compute secondary divisors
nodes.statement:
Next, use part~\ref{ps-comp2} of Proposition~\ref{prop: ps-computation} to
  compute~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$. To ease the computation
  of~$\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}$, perform invertible integer column operations on~$\tilde{L}$ to
  compute its Hermite normal form~$A$. (We will always take ``Hermite normal
  form'' to mean ``column Hermite normal form''.) Then find the set~$S$ of standard
  representatives for the coset $D|_{q=0}+\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}A$ modulo $\prod_{v\in
  V\setminus\left\{ q \right\}}\ell_v\mathbb{Z}$.  Finally~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}=\left\{
  c+kq:c\in S \text{ and } 0\leq k <\ell_q\right\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\mathcal{S}_{[D]}$ via part (2) of Proposition 3.4.

nodes.name: Hermite normal form
nodes.statement:
To ease the computation
  of~$\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}$, perform invertible integer column operations on~$\tilde{L}$ to
  compute its Hermite normal form~$A$. (We will always take ``Hermite normal
  form'' to mean ``column Hermite normal form''.)
nodes.statement_short: Column-reduce $\tilde L$ to Hermite normal form $A$.

nodes.name: Standard representatives
nodes.statement:
Then find the set~$S$ of standard
  representatives for the coset $D|_{q=0}+\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}A$ modulo $\prod_{v\in
  V\setminus\left\{ q \right\}}\ell_v\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: Enumerate standard representatives of the coset $D|_{q=0}+\mathrm{im}A$.

nodes.name: Append q-coordinate
nodes.statement:
Finally~$\mathcal{S}_{[D]}=\left\{
  c+kq:c\in S \text{ and } 0\leq k <\ell_q\right\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Append all $q$-coordinates $0\le k<\ell_q$.

nodes.name: Inequality description
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\mathcal{K}_D$ via $\tilde L$ and the last Laplacian row.

nodes.name: Cone structure
nodes.statement:
Since~$\tilde{L}$ is invertible, these defining conditions are independent, and it
follows that~$\mathcal{K}_D$ is a rational~$n$-cone.
nodes.statement_short: Independent conditions make $\mathcal{K}_D$ a rational $n$-cone.

nodes.name: Compute apex
nodes.statement:
To find the apex, first
solve~$\tilde{L} f=-D|_{q=0}$ to find~$f=\tilde{L}^{-1}(-D|_{q=0})$.  Next, since the sum of the
  rows of~$L$ is~$0$, if follows that~$\tilde{r}_n\cdot f=-\tilde{L} f$, and it is now
  easy to verify that the last coordinate of the apex is~$t=0$ using the fact
  that~$\deg(D)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve $\tilde Lf=-D|_{q=0}$; degree zero gives $t=0$.

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement:
The rest follows immediately from the discussion preceding the theorem.
Part~\ref{poly1} uses the fact that every firing script has a unique
representative modulo $\ker L$ having final coordinate~$0$.
nodes.statement_short: Firing scripts have unique representatives with last coordinate 0.

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement:
Part~\ref{poly2}
relies on Property~\ref{property: characterization}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Property 4.1.

nodes.name: Part (3)
nodes.statement:
Part~\ref{poly3} follows
since~$\deg\psi_D(f,k)=k$.
nodes.statement_short: Degree of $\psi_D(f,k)$ is $k$, giving the generating function.

nodes.name: Describe union
nodes.statement:
We have~$f\in\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D$ if and only if
  \[
    \tilde{L} f\geq-D|_{q=0}\quad\text{and}\quad \tilde{r}_n\cdot f\geq -D(q)-k
  \]
  for some~$k\in\mathbb{N}$.  The second condition is superfluous since~$k$ can
  be arbitrarily large.
nodes.statement_short: Membership reduces to $\tilde Lf\ge-D|_{q=0}$.

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement:
The fact that~$\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}$ is a rational
  simplicial~$(n-1)$-cone with apex~$\tilde{L}^{-1}(-D|_{q=0})$ follows since~$\tilde{L}$ is 
  invertible.  This establishes part~\ref{facet1}.
nodes.statement_short: Invertibility of $\tilde L$ gives a simplicial cone with the stated apex.

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement:
Part~\ref{facet2} then follows from part~\ref{facet1} and the description
  of~$\mathcal{K}_D$ given in~\eqref{eqn: K_D} in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm: poly}.
nodes.statement_short: Use part (1) and equation (4).

nodes.name: Part (3)
nodes.statement:
Since~$K_D=\imath_D{\widetilde{\mathcal{K}}_D}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}q$, part~\ref{facet3} follows from
  Theorem~\ref{thm: poly}~\ref{poly2} and Theorem~\ref{thm: primary-secondary}~\ref{ps-2}.
nodes.statement_short: Use Theorems 4.4(2) and 3.1(2).

nodes.name: Expand in monomials
nodes.statement:
An arbitrary element of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]$ may be written
  as~$f=\sum^{\,}_{E}a_Ex^E$ where the sum is over all effective divisors of~$G$
  and all but finitely many~$a_E$ are zero.
nodes.statement_short: Write $f=\sum a_Ex^E$ over effective divisors.

nodes.name: Compute action
nodes.statement:
Let~$\chi\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)^{*}$.  Then
  \allowdisplaybreaks
  \begin{align*}
    f\circ\rho(\chi)
    &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E(x^E\circ\rho(\chi))\\
    &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E\textstyle\left(\prod_{v\in V}\chi([v-q])^{E(v)} \right)x^E\\
    &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E\textstyle\,\chi\!\left(\sum_{v\in V}E(v)([v-q])\right)x^E\\
    &= \sum_{E}a^{\,}_E\textstyle\,\chi\!\left([E-\deg(E)q]\right)x^E.
  \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $\rho(\chi)$ scales $x^E$ by $\chi([E-\deg(E)q])$.

nodes.name: Characterize invariants
nodes.statement:
Therefore,~$f\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{x}]^{\Gamma}_{[D]}$ if and only if for each~$E$ such
  that~$a^{\,}_E\neq0$, we have $\chi([E-\deg(E)q])=\chi([D])$ for all~$\chi$,
  or equivalently, $[E-\deg(E)q]=[D]$, i.e.,~$E\in\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is $[D]$-relative invariant iff all its monomials lie in $\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
Parts~\ref{inv1},~\ref{inv2}, and~\ref{inv3} follow.  Part~\ref{inv2} reflects
 the fact that the~$\mathbb{E}_{[D]}$ partition the set of effective divisors.
nodes.statement_short: All three parts follow.

nodes.name: Part (1): divisibility equivalence
nodes.statement:
Let~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$, and let~$a=a_N=a_1\dots a_n$ be a representative word
for $\mathrm{code}(N)$.  We first show that~$N$ is~$m_j$-divisible if and only
if~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible.  Let~$\ell$ be the period of~$\mathrm{code}(N)$.  Then since
the length of the necklace~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n$, there is an integer~$p$ such
that~$n=p\ell$.  The period of~$N$ is~$\ell+\alpha$
where~$\alpha:=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}a_i$.  Since~$\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i=k$, and the
period of~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$\ell$, it follows that~$p\alpha=k$.  Therefore,
\begin{align*}
  \text{$N$ is~$m_j$-divisible}&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \left( \frac{n+k}{\gcd(n,k,j)}\right)\bigg|\,(\ell+\alpha)\\[8pt]
  &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{p(\ell+\alpha)}{\gcd(p\ell,p\alpha,j)}\bigg|\,(\ell+\alpha)\\[8pt]
   &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{\gcd(p\ell,p\alpha,j)}{p(\ell+\alpha)}\cdot(\ell+\alpha)\in\mathbb{Z}\\[8pt]
   &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p|j.
\end{align*}
Similarly,
\[
  \text{$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible}
  \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad\left( \frac{n}{\gcd(n,j)} \right)\bigg|\,\ell
  \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\frac{p\ell}{\gcd(p\ell,j)}\bigg|\,\ell
  \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad p|j.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Both divisibility conditions reduce to $p\mid j$.

nodes.name: Fix necklace
nodes.statement:
Let~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$, and let~$a=a_N=a_1\dots a_n$ be a representative word
for $\mathrm{code}(N)$.  We first show that~$N$ is~$m_j$-divisible if and only
if~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $N$ and a code word $a$; state part (1).

nodes.name: Periods
nodes.statement:
Let~$\ell$ be the period of~$\mathrm{code}(N)$.  Then since
the length of the necklace~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n$, there is an integer~$p$ such
that~$n=p\ell$.  The period of~$N$ is~$\ell+\alpha$
where~$\alpha:=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}a_i$.  Since~$\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_i=k$, and the
period of~$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$\ell$, it follows that~$p\alpha=k$.
nodes.statement_short: With $n=p\ell$, the period of $N$ is $\ell+\alpha$ and $p\alpha=k$.

nodes.name: m_j-divisibility
nodes.statement:
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
  \text{$N$ is~$m_j$-divisible}&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \left( \frac{n+k}{\gcd(n,k,j)}\right)\bigg|\,(\ell+\alpha)\\[8pt]
  &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{p(\ell+\alpha)}{\gcd(p\ell,p\alpha,j)}\bigg|\,(\ell+\alpha)\\[8pt]
   &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{\gcd(p\ell,p\alpha,j)}{p(\ell+\alpha)}\cdot(\ell+\alpha)\in\mathbb{Z}\\[8pt]
   &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p|j.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $N$ is $m_j$-divisible iff $p\mid j$.

nodes.name: n_j-divisibility
nodes.statement:
Similarly,
\[
  \text{$\mathrm{code}(N)$ is~$n_j$-divisible}
  \quad \Leftrightarrow\quad\left( \frac{n}{\gcd(n,j)} \right)\bigg|\,\ell
  \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\frac{p\ell}{\gcd(p\ell,j)}\bigg|\,\ell
  \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad p|j.
\]
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{code}(N)$ is $n_j$-divisible iff $p\mid j$.

nodes.name: Part (2): f_N nonzero of degree k
nodes.statement:
Continuing with the notation already established, we now prove part~\ref{basis part2}.  Since~$f_N$ is defined using the Reynolds operator, it
is~$[D_j]$-invariant. To see that it is non-zero, we show that the
monomial~$y^a$ appears in~$f_N$ with a nonzero coefficient. We
have~$y^a=y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ if and only if~$i$ is a multiple of the
period~$\ell$.  However,~$\ell$ is divisible by~$n_j$, which is the order
of~$\omega^{j}$.  So the coefficient of~$y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ in the expression for
the Reynolds operator is~$\omega^{-ij}/n=1/n$.  Therefore, the coefficient
of~$y^{a}$ in~$f_N$ is the integer~$p/n=1/\ell\neq0$.  It now follows that~$f_N$
has degree~$k$.
nodes.statement_short: Each $f_N$ is a nonzero $[D_j]$-invariant of degree $k$.

nodes.name: Invariance
nodes.statement:
Continuing with the notation already established, we now prove part~\ref{basis part2}.  Since~$f_N$ is defined using the Reynolds operator, it
is~$[D_j]$-invariant.
nodes.statement_short: $f_N$ is invariant by construction via the Reynolds operator.

nodes.name: Nonvanishing
nodes.statement:
To see that it is non-zero, we show that the
monomial~$y^a$ appears in~$f_N$ with a nonzero coefficient. We
have~$y^a=y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ if and only if~$i$ is a multiple of the
period~$\ell$.  However,~$\ell$ is divisible by~$n_j$, which is the order
of~$\omega^{j}$.  So the coefficient of~$y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ in the expression for
the Reynolds operator is~$\omega^{-ij}/n=1/n$.  Therefore, the coefficient
of~$y^{a}$ in~$f_N$ is the integer~$p/n=1/\ell\neq0$.  It now follows that~$f_N$
has degree~$k$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $y^a$ has nonzero coefficient in $f_N$.

nodes.name: Coefficient computation
nodes.statement:
We
have~$y^a=y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ if and only if~$i$ is a multiple of the
period~$\ell$.  However,~$\ell$ is divisible by~$n_j$, which is the order
of~$\omega^{j}$.  So the coefficient of~$y^{\sigma^i(a)}$ in the expression for
the Reynolds operator is~$\omega^{-ij}/n=1/n$.
nodes.statement_short: Shifts fixing $a$ are multiples of $\ell$, on which $\omega^{-ij}=1$.

nodes.name: Nonzero coefficient
nodes.statement:
Therefore, the coefficient
of~$y^{a}$ in~$f_N$ is the integer~$p/n=1/\ell\neq0$.  It now follows that~$f_N$
has degree~$k$.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficient is $1/\ell\neq0$, so $f_N$ has degree $k$.

nodes.name: Spanning
nodes.statement:
Let~$\mathcal{B}$ be the set of~$f_N$ as~$N$ varies over~$m_j$-divisible
elements of~$\mathcal{N}(n,k)$.  Distinct elements of~$\mathcal{B}$ share no monomials
in common, and hence~$\mathcal{B}$ is a linearly independent set.  To
show~$\mathcal{B}$ spans the relative invariant module and finish the
proof, let~$h\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ be a
homogeneous~$[D_j]$-invariant of degree~$k$. For the sake of contradiction,
suppose~$h\notin\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$.  We regard~$h$ as a sum of terms where each
term is a nonzero constant times a monomial, and the monomials are distinct.
Among all elements of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ that are
not in~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$, let~$h$ be one with the fewest number of terms, and
let~~$\beta y^b$ be one of these terms. Then~$\beta\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)$ is a
sum of terms appearing in~$h$.  Let~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ be the necklace
with~$\mathrm{code}(N)=[b]$.  Say~$[b]$ has period~$m$ and write~$n=mq$ for some
integer~$q$.  The coefficient of~$y^b$ in~$\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)$ is
\[
  \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^q(\omega^{-jm})^i,
\]
and the order of~$\omega^{-jm}$ is~$q/\gcd(q,j)$, a divisor of~$q$.
If~$[b]$ is not~$n_j$-divisible, then the order of~$\omega^j$ does not
divide~$m$, and hence,~$\omega^{jm}\neq1$.  It would then follow that the above sum
is~$0$, which contradicts the fact that~$\beta y^b$ is a term of~$h$.
Therefore,~$[b]$ is~$n_j$-divisible
and~$\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)=f_N\in\mathcal{B}$.  However, then the polynomial~$h-\beta f_N$
is an element of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ with fewer terms
than~$h$ and not in~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$, which is a contradiction.
So~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})=\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{B}$ is independent and spans, by a minimal counterexample.

nodes.name: Independence
nodes.statement:
Let~$\mathcal{B}$ be the set of~$f_N$ as~$N$ varies over~$m_j$-divisible
elements of~$\mathcal{N}(n,k)$.  Distinct elements of~$\mathcal{B}$ share no monomials
in common, and hence~$\mathcal{B}$ is a linearly independent set.
nodes.statement_short: Distinct $f_N$ share no monomials.

nodes.name: Assume not spanning
nodes.statement:
To
show~$\mathcal{B}$ spans the relative invariant module and finish the
proof, let~$h\in\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ be a
homogeneous~$[D_j]$-invariant of degree~$k$. For the sake of contradiction,
suppose~$h\notin\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose some invariant $h$ is outside the span.

nodes.name: Minimal counterexample
nodes.statement:
We regard~$h$ as a sum of terms where each
term is a nonzero constant times a monomial, and the monomials are distinct.
Among all elements of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ that are
not in~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$, let~$h$ be one with the fewest number of terms, and
let~~$\beta y^b$ be one of these terms. Then~$\beta\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)$ is a
sum of terms appearing in~$h$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $h$ with fewest terms and a term $\beta y^b$.

nodes.name: Coefficient of y^b
nodes.statement:
Let~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ be the necklace
with~$\mathrm{code}(N)=[b]$.  Say~$[b]$ has period~$m$ and write~$n=mq$ for some
integer~$q$.  The coefficient of~$y^b$ in~$\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)$ is
\[
  \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^q(\omega^{-jm})^i,
\]
and the order of~$\omega^{-jm}$ is~$q/\gcd(q,j)$, a divisor of~$q$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the coefficient of $y^b$ in $\mathcal{R}(y^b)$ as a root-of-unity sum.

nodes.name: Divisibility of [b]
nodes.statement:
If~$[b]$ is not~$n_j$-divisible, then the order of~$\omega^j$ does not
divide~$m$, and hence,~$\omega^{jm}\neq1$.  It would then follow that the above sum
is~$0$, which contradicts the fact that~$\beta y^b$ is a term of~$h$.
Therefore,~$[b]$ is~$n_j$-divisible
and~$\mathcal{R}_{[D_j]}(y^b)=f_N\in\mathcal{B}$.
nodes.statement_short: Non-divisibility would kill the term, so $\mathcal{R}(y^b)=f_N\in\mathcal{B}$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement:
However, then the polynomial~$h-\beta f_N$
is an element of~$\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$ with fewer terms
than~$h$ and not in~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})$, which is a contradiction.
So~$\mathrm{Span}(\mathcal{B})=\mathbb{C}[\mathbf{y}]^{\Gamma'}_{[D_j],k}$.
nodes.statement_short: $h-\beta f_N$ is a smaller counterexample; hence $\mathcal{B}$ spans.

nodes.name: Laplacian columns
nodes.statement:
First note that if~$c$ is a column of the Laplacian matrix
for~$C_n$, then~$c\cdot\eta=0\bmod n$.
nodes.statement_short: Each Laplacian column is orthogonal to $\eta$ mod $n$.

nodes.name: Compute invariants
nodes.statement:
Given any~$D\in\mathrm{Div}(C_n)$, there
exists~$i$ and~$m$ such that~$D\sim D_i+mq$.  Then~$D\cdot\vec{1}=m$, and
\[
  D\cdot\eta = (D_i+mq)\cdot\eta\bmod n= i\bmod n.
\]
The result follows.
nodes.statement_short: For $D\sim D_i+mq$, $D\cdot\vec1=m$ and $D\cdot\eta\equiv i$.

nodes.name: Injectivity setup
nodes.statement:
Let~$\eta=(1,2,\dots,n)$ as in Lemma~\ref{lemma: divisors on C_n}.
  To show injectivity, suppose~$\psi(E)=\psi(E')$ for some pair of
  effective divisors~$E,E'\in\mathrm{Div}^k(C_n)$.  It follows that~$E'=\sigma^i(E)$ for
  some~$i$.
nodes.statement_short: Equal necklaces give $E'=\sigma^i(E)$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 6.6
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lemma: divisors on C_n}, working modulo~$n$,
  \[
    j = E'\cdot\eta =\sigma^i(E)\cdot\eta=E\cdot(\eta+i\vec{1})=j+ik\bmod n.
  \]
nodes.statement_short: Rotation shifts $E\cdot\eta$ by $ik$.

nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: If~$\gcd(n,k)=1$, it follows that~$i=0\bmod n$, and hence~$E=E'$.
nodes.statement_short: Coprimality forces $i\equiv0$.

nodes.name: Surjectivity setup
nodes.statement:
For surjectivity, let~$N\in\mathcal{N}(n,k)$ with~$\mathrm{code}(N)=[a_1\dots a_n]$.
  Let~$E:=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathrm{Div}^k(C_n)$, and say~$E\cdot\eta=m\bmod n$.
  Then $\sigma^i(E)\cdot\eta=m+ik\bmod n$ for each~$i$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $E$ from the code of $N$; rotations shift $E\cdot\eta$ by $k$.

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement:
If~$\gcd(n,k)=1$,
  we can take~$i$ so that~$m+ik=j\bmod n$ and define~$E':=\sigma^i(E)$.
  Then~$E'\in|D_j+kq|$ and~$\psi(E')=N$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $i$ with $m+ik\equiv j$; then $\sigma^i(E)\in|D_j+kq|$.

nodes.name: Diagonalize
nodes.statement:
To compute with Corollary~\ref{cor: lambda-molien} concretely,  use
integer row and column operations to reduce~$\tilde{L}$ to diagonal form (e.g., Smith
normal form), denoting the result by~$M:=\mathrm{diag}(m_1,\dots,m_{n-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce $\tilde L$ to Smith normal form $M$.

nodes.name: Record transforms
nodes.statement:
Record the
row and column operations in matrices~$U$ and~$W$ so that~$U\tilde{L} W = M$.
nodes.statement_short: Record $U,W$ with $U\tilde LW=M$.

nodes.name: Identify Jac with R
nodes.statement:
Then~$U$ descends to an isomorphism
\[
  \mathrm{Jac}(G)\simeq\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}/\mathrm{im}_{\mathbb{Z}}\tilde{L}\xrightarrow{\ U\ }\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\mathbb{Z}/m_i\mathbb{Z}.
\]
Having identified~$\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ with~$R:=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\mathbb{Z}/m_i\mathbb{Z}$, we now describe
the characters.
nodes.statement_short: $U$ identifies $\mathrm{Jac}(G)$ with $R=\prod\mathbb{Z}/m_i$.

nodes.name: Lift r
nodes.statement:
For each~$r\in R$, choose a representative
lifting~$(r_1,\dots,r_{n-1})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$, and let $ \tilde{r} :=
\left(\frac{r_1}{m_1},\dots,\frac{r_{n-1}}{m_{n-1}} \right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift $r$ and scale by $1/m_i$.

nodes.name: Characters of R
nodes.statement:
Define the
character~$\tilde{\chi}_r\in R^*$ by
\[
  \tilde{\chi}_r(a) :=\exp(2\pi i\,(\tilde{r}\cdot a))
\]
for each~$a\in R$.
nodes.statement_short: $\tilde\chi_r(a)=\exp(2\pi i\,\tilde r\cdot a)$.

nodes.name: Characters of Jac
nodes.statement:
Then define~$\chi_r\in\mathrm{Jac}^*(G)$
by
\[
  \chi_r([D]):=\tilde{\chi}_r(U(D|_{q=0}))
\]
for each~$[D]\in\mathrm{Jac}(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pull back via $U$.

nodes.name: Representation matrices
nodes.statement:
It follows that
\[
  \rho(\chi_r)=\mathrm{diag}(\tilde{\chi}_r(u_1),\tilde{\chi}_r(u_2),\dots,\tilde{\chi}_r(u_{n-1}),1)
\]
where~$u_j$ is the~$j$-th column of~$U$.
nodes.statement_short: $\rho(\chi_r)$ is diagonal with entries $\tilde\chi_r(u_j)$.

nodes.name: Drop trivial factors
nodes.statement:
In all of the above, if~$m_k=1$ for
some~$k$, then the~$k$-th factor of~$R$ and the~$k$-th {\em row} of~$U$ may be
dropped.
nodes.statement_short: Discard factors with $m_k=1$.
